items.title: 52300_Trummy Young oral history interview
items.q: See, I stayed with Louis from 1952 to about February of -- first part of '64.

ctx.x: I said, no, I got to go home. My wife is sick. And so it's a good thing I did because I found out my wife had cancer, and we caught it, you know, just in time. She went out to this White Memorial Hospital out here, and I used to take her out there for cobalt treatments.

And so this was May of '64. See, I stayed with Louis from 1952 to about February of -- first part of '64. And after she completed her treatments, the doctor said, well, there's no more I can do. We just have to wait and see how

she comes along. So they gave us permission to move, and we -- I sold my home. We went back to Honolulu, and I'd been living back there since, you know, but I found out that, had I stayed on the road and accepted more money, well, my wife would have been gone, you know?

items.title: Louis Armstrong Interview, 1960-08-09
items.q: And Trummy and I, we handled up Tiger Rags

ctx.x: Do you think your audience in Caracas was as responsive to jazz, or to American jazz, as those audiences in Europe and in the United States? Everywhere in the world. Everywhere.

It's the same. Notes and notes in any language. Now, let me tell you a thing. At the time we was there, they was having that little scrimmage. The president, what, blah, blah, you know what's happening. And they were supposed to bomb the university where we played that night. Yeah. And there wasn't a student thinking about it. Sure. Then nothing happened. We played for the president's party. Nothing happened. And we played after that in a hotel downtown, Pack House. And then we played in the bullring, concerts…
Do you think there are different kinds of jazz? He said he spoke about American jazz with his friends and German jazz.
